Module 08 / Physics 2

Magnetic fields: the cross product fixes the direction

Magnetic forces, current-loop torque, wire fields, and Ampere law.

Topics in this module
Force on a moving charge and on a wireCircular and helical motion: derived extensionsTorque on a current loopLong wires, parallel-current force, and Ampere's lawSolenoids, cores, and scope of symmetryMagnetism, field notation, and the three right-hand rulesSolve both source magnetic-force examples in fullTorque: derive the area factor and use the actual angleSource-wire fields, parallel-wire force, and solenoidsWorked applications: models, calculations, and interpretation

Like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract. Breaking a bar magnet makes smaller dipoles, not isolated ordinary north and south poles. Outside a bar magnet, conventional field lines go north to south; they continue through the magnet to form closed loops. A compass's north-seeking end gives the local field direction. Earth's geographic and magnetic pole descriptions are not identical.

Oersted's current-carrying wire deflects a compass, showing that current creates a magnetic field. Do not confuse this source-field right-hand grip rule with the force cross-product rule.

Force on a moving charge and on a wire

FB=qv×B,FB=∣q∣vBsin⁡θ.\mathbf F_B=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B,\quad F_B=|q|vB\sin\theta.FB​=qv×B,FB​=∣q∣vBsinθ.

θ\thetaθ is between velocity and B. For positive q, curl the right-hand direction from v toward B; reverse the result for negative q. A charge at rest has no magnetic force from this law. Parallel or antiparallel motion gives zero magnetic force, not maximum force. Perpendicular motion gives the maximum magnitude.

Derive wire force. A segment of length L and cross-sectional area A contains nAL carriers. Each has transverse force qvd×Bqv_{d} \times Bqvd​×B. Sum and use I=n∣q∣AvdI = n \left| q \right| Av_{d}I=n∣q∣Avd​ to obtain F=IL×BF = IL \times BF=IL×B, with L directed along conventional current. For a curved wire use I∫dl×BI \int dl \times BI∫dl×B. Only the length inside the field contributes.

Worked example — primary p. 14. I=5.0 AI = 5.0\,\mathrm{A}I=5.0A east; L=1.0 mL = 1.0\,\mathrm{m}L=1.0m; B=1.20 TB = 1.20\,\mathrm{T}B=1.20T at 45° north of east. F=5×1×1.2sin⁡45∘=4.243 NF = 5 \times 1 \times 1.2 \sin 45^{\circ} = 4.243\,\mathrm{N}F=5×1×1.2sin45∘=4.243N. East × north points up in an east/north/up coordinate system.

Worked example — primary p. 20. An electron moves +x at 8.0×106 ms8.0 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}8.0×106sm​. A 0.025 T0.025\,\mathrm{T}0.025T field makes 60° to +x in the +y half of the xy plane. Magnitude: evBsin⁡60∘=2.775×10−14 Ne v B \sin 60^{\circ} = 2.775 \times 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{N}evBsin60∘=2.775×10−14N. Since +x×+y=+z+ x \times + y = + z+x×+y=+z, the electron's force is −z. Without specifying the y-half-plane, the angle alone does not fix that sign.

Circular and helical motion: derived extensions

A magnetic force does no work on a point charge because v⋅(v×B)=0v \cdot \left( v \times B \right) = 0v⋅(v×B)=0. It changes direction, not speed, in a purely magnetic uniform field. For perpendicular motion, set ∣q∣vB=mv2r\left| q \right| vB = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}∣q∣vB=rmv2​:

r=mv⊥∣q∣B,ωc=∣q∣Bm,T=2πm∣q∣B.r=\frac{mv_\perp}{|q|B},\quad \omega_c=\frac{|q|B}{m},\quad T=\frac{2\pi m}{|q|B}.r=∣q∣Bmv⊥​​,ωc​=m∣q∣B​,T=∣q∣B2πm​.

For an oblique entry, v∥v_{\parallel}v∥​ remains constant, while v⊥v_{\perp}v⊥​ circles. Helical pitch: p=v∥Tp=v_{\parallel}Tp=v∥​T. These are nonrelativistic formulas. Combining kinetic energy K with r gives r=(2mK)(∣q∣B)r = \frac{\sqrt{\left( 2 mK \right)}}{\left( \left| q \right| B \right)}r=(∣q∣B)(2mK)​​ for perpendicular entry. In crossed perpendicular E and B fields, straight undeflected motion requires ∣q∣E=∣q∣vB\left| q \right| E = \left| q \right| vB∣q∣E=∣q∣vB, so v=EBv = \frac{E}{B}v=BE​ with force directions opposing.

Torque on a current loop

Opposite sides of a loop in uniform B have equal and opposite forces. Net force can vanish while torque remains. The lever-arm geometry yields:

μ=NIA,τ=μ×B,τ=NIABsin⁡θ,U=−μ⋅B.\begin{gathered}\boldsymbol\mu=NI\mathbf A,\\\boldsymbol\tau=\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B,\\\tau=NIAB\sin\theta,\\U=-\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\mathbf B.\end{gathered}μ=NIA,τ=μ×B,τ=NIABsinθ,U=−μ⋅B.​

Here θ\thetaθ is between the AREA NORMAL and B, not between the loop's plane and B. For angle ϕ\phiϕ to the plane, sin⁡θ=cos⁡ϕ\sin \theta = \cos \phisinθ=cosϕ. Maximum torque occurs when the normal is perpendicular to B. Zero torque occurs when the normal is parallel or antiparallel; the parallel orientation has the lower potential energy.

Worked example — primary p. 28. Diameter: 20.0 cm20.0\,\mathrm{cm}20.0cm, so r=0.100 mr = 0.100\,\mathrm{m}r=0.100m and A=π(0.100)2A = \pi \left( 0.100 \right)^{2}A=π(0.100)2. With N=10N = 10N=10, I=3.00 AI = 3.00\,\mathrm{A}I=3.00A, B=2.00 TB = 2.00\,\mathrm{T}B=2.00T, τmax=1.885 N⋅m\tau _{\mathrm{max}} = 1.885\,\mathrm{N} \cdot mτmax​=1.885N⋅m and τmin=0\tau _{\mathrm{min}} = 0τmin​=0. The primary's side-force label involving IAB should not be read as the wire-force law: force uses a LENGTH, while torque uses an AREA.

A galvanometer turns a current-carrying coil against a restoring effect. Analog meters build on that principle. A motor converts electrical energy to mechanical energy; a loudspeaker moves a coil and cone with a varying force.

Long wires, parallel-current force, and Ampere's law

Magnetostatic Ampere's law is ∮B⋅dl=μ0Ienclosed\oint B \cdot dl = \mu_{0} I_{\mathrm{enclosed}}∮B⋅dl=μ0​Ienclosed​. For a long straight wire, cylindrical symmetry makes B constant on a circular path. Therefore B(2πr)=μ0IB \left( 2 \pi r \right) = \mu_{0} IB(2πr)=μ0​I:

B=μ0I2πr,FL=I2B1=μ0I1I22πd.B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r},\quad \frac FL=I_2B_1=\frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2}{2\pi d}.B=2πrμ0​I​,LF​=I2​B1​=2πdμ0​I1​I2​​.

Use μ0≈4π×10−7 T⋅mA\mu_{0} \approx \frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{T} \cdot m}{A}μ0​≈A4π×10−7T⋅m​ for course calculations. Same-direction parallel currents attract; opposite directions repel. The distance is between the wire axes, not wire length. Fields from several wires add as vectors.

Worked examples — primary pp. 33 and 36. A 25 A25\,\mathrm{A}25A upward wire at r=0.10 mr = 0.10\,\mathrm{m}r=0.10m gives B=5.0×10−5 TB = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}B=5.0×10−5T. At a point north of that wire, the direction is west. Two wires carrying 8.0 A8.0\,\mathrm{A}8.0A, separated by 0.0030 m0.0030\,\mathrm{m}0.0030m over 2.0 m2.0\,\mathrm{m}2.0m length, exert F=8.533×10−3 NF = 8.533 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N}F=8.533×10−3N. Their relative current directions determine attraction or repulsion.

Solenoids, cores, and scope of symmetry

For an ideal long solenoid, an Amperian rectangle has negligible external contribution. Enclosed current is (Nℓ)I\left( \frac{N}{\ell} \right) I(ℓN​)I times its interior path length. Thus B=μ0(Nℓ)IB = \mu_{0} \left( \frac{N}{\ell} \right) IB=μ0​(ℓN​)I, or μnI\mu nIμnI in an ideal linear core. ℓ is the SOLENOID length, not the total winding-wire length.

Worked example — primary p. 39. N=420N = 420N=420, ℓ=0.12 m\ell = 0.12\,\mathrm{m}ℓ=0.12m, I=2.0 AI = 2.0\,\mathrm{A}I=2.0A. B=4π×10−7(4200.12)(2)=8.796×10−3 T\begin{aligned}B &= 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \left( \frac{420}{0.12} \right) \left( 2 \right) \\&= 8.796 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{T}\end{aligned}B​=4π×10−7(0.12420​)(2)=8.796×10−3T​ near the center in the long-solenoid approximation.

An iron core can increase field strongly, but a constant relative permeability is only an approximation; real cores can saturate and show hysteresis. Ampere's law alone does not let you pull B outside the integral without sufficient symmetry. For a circular coil's center, a separate Biot–Savart integration gives B=μ0NI(2R)B = \frac{\mu_{0} NI}{\left( 2 R \right)}B=(2R)μ0​NI​; do not substitute the long-solenoid formula into a single-loop problem.

Derive the circular-coil result. Biot–Savart gives dB=μ0Idlsin⁡θ(4πr2)dB = \frac{\mu_{0} I dl \sin \theta}{\left( 4 \pi r^{2} \right)}dB=(4πr2)μ0​Idlsinθ​. At a loop's center, r=Rr = Rr=R and every tangent element is perpendicular to its radius. All field contributions point along the same axis. Integrate dl around circumference 2πR and multiply by N:

Bcenter=μ0NI4πR2∮dl=μ0NI4πR2(2πR)=μ0NI2R.B_{center}=\frac{\mu_0NI}{4\pi R^2}\oint dl=\frac{\mu_0NI}{4\pi R^2}(2\pi R)=\frac{\mu_0NI}{2R}.Bcenter​=4πR2μ0​NI​∮dl=4πR2μ0​NI​(2πR)=2Rμ0​NI​.

For 20 turns, 0.050 m0.050\,\mathrm{m}0.050m radius, and 2.0 A2.0\,\mathrm{A}2.0A, B≈5.027×10−4 TB \approx 5.027 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}B≈5.027×10−4T. This formula describes thin coincident loops. A long coil uses the solenoid approximation instead. A magnetic field created by this coil can exert force on another wire; do not substitute the wire's own field into a simple external-field force calculation.

Use mp=1.67×10−27 kgm_{p} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}mp​=1.67×10−27kg and e=1.602×10−19 Ce = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}e=1.602×10−19C. Its radius is 0.05212 m0.05212\,\mathrm{m}0.05212m and period is 3.275×10−7 s3.275 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{s}3.275×10−7s. Magnetism, field notation, and the three right-hand rules

Source context — primary pp. 4–11. The historical material describes magnetite and the name Magnesia. A magnetized needle aligns with the local field. Either end of a magnet can attract an initially unmagnetized iron nail because the nail becomes magnetized. Splitting a magnet produces smaller dipoles. It does not separate an ordinary bar magnet into isolated north and south poles.

Earth and a compass. The geographic poles describe the rotation axis. Magnetic-pole locations and the local field direction differ from that axis. Near geographic north, Earth's field can attract a compass's north-seeking end. Keep the pole-naming convention separate from the field direction used in a force calculation.

Physical quantity Right-hand operation What the result means
Field around a straight wire Point the thumb along conventional current; curl the fingers Finger curl gives B around the wire
Force on a current-carrying segment Form L×BL \times BL×B, with L along conventional current The cross product gives the force direction
Force on a moving positive charge Form v×Bv \times Bv×B The result gives force for positive q
Force on a negative charge Find v×Bv \times Bv×B, then reverse it Reversal accounts for negative q

Use a dot ⊙ for a vector out of the page and a cross ⊗ for a vector into the page. In a right-handed coordinate system, x×y=zx \times y = zx×y=z, y×z=xy \times z = xy×z=x, and z×x=yz \times x = yz×x=y. Reversing either factor reverses the cross product.

Units. 1 T=1 NAm=1 N⋅s(C⋅m)=1 Wbm2\begin{aligned}1\,\mathrm{T} &= 1\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{A} \mathrm{m}} \\&= \frac{1\,\mathrm{N} \cdot s}{\left( C \cdot m \right)} \\&= \frac{1\,\mathrm{Wb}}{m^{2}}\end{aligned}1T​=1AmN​=(C⋅m)1N⋅s​=m21Wb​​ Also, 1 T=1041\,\mathrm{T} = 10^{4}1T=104 gauss. Convert 3.0 mm3.0\,\mathrm{mm}3.0mm to 0.0030 m0.0030\,\mathrm{m}0.0030m before using a wire-spacing formula.

Derivation∴

Wire-force law from the motion of charge carriers

Source laws: Primary pp. 12–17. Let the carrier number density be n, wire cross section A, and segment length L. Use a uniform external field.

  1. Count the carriers inside the segment: Ncarriers=nALN_{\mathrm{carriers}} = nALNcarriers​=nAL.
  2. Add their magnetic forces: Ftotal=nALq(vd×B)F_{\mathrm{total}} = nALq \left( v_{d} \times B \right)Ftotal​=nALq(vd​×B).
  3. Use the signed carrier-current relation nqvd=Jnqv_{d} = Jnqvd​=J, with conventional-current direction encoded in J.
  4. Replace JA by the current and direct the length vector along that current.
F=IL×B,F=ILBsin⁡θ.\mathbf F=I\mathbf L\times\mathbf B, \qquad F=ILB\sin\theta.F=IL×B,F=ILBsinθ.

This derivation removes the microscopic carrier density and drift speed. L means the length inside the field. For a curved path in a nonuniform field, integrate Idl×BI dl \times BIdl×B instead of using one segment's product.

Magnetic force on the television-tube electron

Source: Primary p. 20. Given: v=8.0×106 msv = 8.0 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}v=8.0×106sm​ along +x, B=0.025 TB = 0.025\,\mathrm{T}B=0.025T at 60° to +x in the xy plane. Use ∣q∣=1.602×10−19 C\left| q \right| = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}∣q∣=1.602×10−19C.

  1. Calculate the perpendicular field component: Bperp=Bsin⁡60∘=0.0216506 TB_{\mathrm{perp}} = B\sin 60^{\circ} = 0.0216506\,\mathrm{T}Bperp​=Bsin60∘=0.0216506T.

Derivation∴

Recover an unknown field or angle from a force measurement

Start with F=∣q∣vBsin⁡θF = \left| q \right| vB\sin \thetaF=∣q∣vBsinθ or F=ILBsin⁡θF = ILB\sin \thetaF=ILBsinθ. If the geometry is perpendicular, sin⁡θ=1\sin \theta = 1sinθ=1.

B=F∣q∣vsin⁡θ,v=F∣q∣Bsin⁡θ,sin⁡θ=F∣q∣vB.B=\frac{F}{|q|v\sin\theta},\qquad v=\frac{F}{|q|B\sin\theta},\qquad \sin\theta=\frac{F}{|q|vB}.B=∣q∣vsinθF​,v=∣q∣BsinθF​,sinθ=∣q∣vBF​.

For a wire, replace |q|v by IL. A sine value larger than one signals inconsistent data or a wrong equation. In 0°–180°, both θ\thetaθ and 180∘−θ180^{\circ} - \theta180∘−θ have the same sine. Magnitude data alone cannot distinguish those directions. Parallel motion gives zero force even in a nonzero field.

Torque: derive the area factor and use the actual angle

Derivation∴

Why a current loop has torque NIABsin⁡θNIAB\sin \thetaNIABsinθ

Sources: Primary pp. 25–28. Let a rectangular loop have side length a along one pair of opposite forces and separation b between them.

  1. Each active side feels force F=IaBF = IaBF=IaB for the perpendicular-field component in the stated geometry.
  2. The perpendicular lever arm between the forces is bsin⁡θb\sin \thetabsinθ, where θ\thetaθ measures the area normal relative to B.
  3. Add the two moments as a force couple: τ=F(bsin⁡θ)\tau = F \left( b\sin \theta \right)τ=F(bsinθ).
  4. Substitute A=abA = abA=ab and multiply by N turns.
τ=NIabBsin⁡θ=NIABsin⁡θ.\tau=NIabB\sin\theta=NIAB\sin\theta.τ=NIabBsinθ=NIABsinθ.

Equal and opposite side forces can cancel the net force while their torques add. Primary p. 27's side-force expression “IAB” uses area where a length is needed. Force uses ILB; torque uses NIAB.

  4. Set the area normal perpendicular to B for the maximum. Set it parallel or antiparallel for τmin=0\tau _{\mathrm{min}} = 0τmin​=0.
  5. For a labeled extension at θ=30∘\theta = 30^{\circ}θ=30∘ to the normal, τ=τmaxsin⁡30∘=0.942478 N⋅m\tau = \tau _{\mathrm{max}}\sin 30^{\circ} = 0.942478\,\mathrm{N} \cdot mτ=τmax​sin30∘=0.942478N⋅m.

Derivation∴

Magnetic-loop potential energy from the torque

This is a labeled extension of the source's torque model. Keep the current, loop area, and applied field constant, so μ=NIA\mu = NIAμ=NIA stays constant. The magnetic torque turns a loop toward alignment with B. Its signed angular component is τmag=−μBsin⁡θ\tau _{\mathrm{mag}} = - \mu B\sin \thetaτmag​=−μBsinθ when positive θ\thetaθ increases the normal-to-field angle.

For a quasistatic increase dθd\thetadθ, an external agent supplies τexternal=+μBsin⁡θ\tau _{\mathrm{external}} = + \mu B\sin \thetaτexternal​=+μBsinθ. Thus dU=τexternaldθdU = \tau _{\mathrm{external}}d\thetadU=τexternal​dθ. Integrating and choosing zero energy at θ=90∘\theta = 90^{\circ}θ=90∘ gives U=−μBcos⁡θU = - \mu B\cos \thetaU=−μBcosθ. Alignment at θ=0\theta = 0θ=0 has minimum energy −μB- \mu B−μB. Anti-alignment at θ=π\theta = \piθ=π has maximum energy +μB+ \mu B+μB. Both have zero torque, but only the first is a stable orientation in this simple model.

Devices — primary pp. 29–31. A galvanometer balances magnetic torque against a restoring torque. In a linear spring model, κtorsionϕ=NIAB\kappa _{\mathrm{torsion}}\phi = NIABκtorsion​ϕ=NIAB for a radial-field meter, so its deflection can indicate current. A motor uses continuing electromagnetic torque to produce rotation. A loudspeaker uses a coil's magnetic force to move its attached cone. An ohmmeter also needs an internal source and associated circuitry; the galvanometer alone does not directly measure resistance.

Field north of an upward 25 A25\,\mathrm{A}25A wire

Parallel-wire force and its attraction or repulsion

F2=μ0I1I2L2πd,FL=μ0I1I22πd.F_2=\frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2L}{2\pi d},\qquad \frac FL=\frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2}{2\pi d}.F2​=2πdμ0​I1​I2​L​,LF​=2πdμ0​I1​I2​​.

Use the grip rule for B1B_{1}B1​, then L2×B1L_{2} \times B_{1}L2​×B1​ for the second force. Matching current directions give forces toward each other. Opposite current directions give forces away from each other. Repeating the calculation on wire 1 gives the same force magnitude.

Derivation∴

Ampere's law inside a long solenoid

Sources: Primary pp. 37–42. Use a rectangular Amperian path with an interior segment of length x parallel to the solenoid axis.

  1. The transverse path segments have B perpendicular to dl, so their dot-product contributions vanish.
  2. Neglect the outside field in the ideal long-solenoid approximation.
  3. The interior segment contributes Bx.
  4. If n=Nℓn = \frac{N}{\ell}n=ℓN​ is turns per unit solenoid length, the path encloses nx turns. Its enclosed current is nxI.
  5. Apply Ampere's law and cancel x.
Bx=μ0(nxI)⇒B=μ0nI=μ0NℓI.Bx=\mu_0(nxI)\Rightarrow B=\mu_0nI =\mu_0\frac{N}{\ell}I.Bx=μ0​(nxI)⇒B=μ0​nI=μ0​ℓN​I.

The Amperian-path length x cancels. The physical solenoid length ℓ remains. It is not the total length of wire used in the winding.

Worked solution↳

The source's 420-turn solenoid

Source: Primary p. 39. Given: N=420N = 420N=420, ℓ=12 cm=0.12 m\ell = 12\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.12\,\mathrm{m}ℓ=12cm=0.12m, and I=2.0 AI = 2.0\,\mathrm{A}I=2.0A.

  1. Calculate the turn density n=Nℓ=3500 m−1n = \frac{N}{\ell} = 3500\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}n=ℓN​=3500m−1.
  2. Calculate B=(4π×10−7)(3500)(2.0)=0.00879646 T\begin{aligned}B &= \left( 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \right) \left( 3500 \right) \left( 2.0 \right) \\&= 0.00879646\,\mathrm{T}\end{aligned}B​=(4π×10−7)(3500)(2.0)=0.00879646T​
  3. Report about 8.80 mT near the center under the long-solenoid model.

Core check. A linear material of relative permeability μr\mu rμr would multiply this ideal value by μr\mu rμr. A real iron core can saturate, so a constant multiplier is not universal.

Worked applications: models, calculations, and interpretation

These worked examples apply the module concepts. Each example states its conditions, explains the model, and shows the complete working.

Worked application 1: Helical motion and magnetic work

A charged particle enters a uniform, static magnetic field with nonzero velocity components parallel and perpendicular to the field. No other force acts.

The parallel and perpendicular velocity components explain the helical path and the constant speed.

  1. Separate the components.
v∥=vcos⁡θ,v⊥=vsin⁡θv_\parallel=v\cos\theta,\quad v_\perp=v\sin\thetav∥​=vcosθ,v⊥​=vsinθ
  1. Check power.
P=q(v⃗×B⃗)⋅v⃗=0P=q(\vec v\times\vec B)\cdot\vec v=0P=q(v×B)⋅v=0
  1. Write the radius.
r=mv⊥/(∣q∣B)r=mv_\perp/(|q|B)r=mv⊥​/(∣q∣B)
  1. Combine the motions. Uniform parallel motion and circular perpendicular motion produce a helix.

Result: The path is helical; speed and kinetic energy remain constant.

Worked application 2: Compare radii at equal kinetic energy

Two nonrelativistic particles have the same charge magnitude and kinetic energy. Their masses are m and 2m. They enter the same uniform magnetic field perpendicularly.

The radius ratio compares the heavier particle with the lighter particle at equal kinetic energy and charge magnitude.

  1. Relate speed to energy.
K=12mv2 ⇒ mv=2mKK=\tfrac12mv^2\ \Rightarrow\ mv=\sqrt{2mK}K=21​mv2 ⇒ mv=2mK​
  1. Use the magnetic radius.
r=mv∣q∣B=2mK∣q∣Br=\frac{mv}{|q|B}=\frac{\sqrt{2mK}}{|q|B}r=∣q∣Bmv​=∣q∣B2mK​​
  1. Take the ratio.
r2m/rm=2r_{2m}/r_m=\sqrt2r2m​/rm​=2​
  1. Check the conditions. The result uses perpendicular, nonrelativistic motion and equal charge magnitudes.

Result: 2\sqrt22​

Worked application 3: Changing only the charge sign

A particle’s charge changes from +q to −q. Mass, initial velocity, and the uniform magnetic field stay the same. The velocity is perpendicular to the field.

Reversing the charge sign reverses the magnetic-force direction while preserving the radius magnitude under the stated conditions.

  1. Reverse the force direction.
F⃗=(−q)(v⃗×B⃗)\vec F=(-q)(\vec v\times\vec B)F=(−q)(v×B)
  1. Compare the radius.
r=mv/(∣q∣B)r=mv/(|q|B)r=mv/(∣q∣B)
  1. Compare the period.
T=2πm/(∣q∣B)T=2\pi m/(|q|B)T=2πm/(∣q∣B)
  1. Interpret the motion. The particle bends in the opposite direction with the same speed and geometric radius.

Result: Curvature reverses; radius and period stay the same.

Worked application 4: Loop plane versus loop normal

A current loop lies with its plane parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The loop current is nonzero.

The loop orientation determines the torque relative to its maximum possible magnitude.

  1. Identify the angle in the law. Use the angle between the field and loop normal.

  2. Convert the stated plane orientation.

θnormal=90∘\theta_{\mathrm{normal}}=90^\circθnormal​=90∘
  1. Evaluate torque.
τ=NIABsin⁡90∘=NIAB\tau=NIAB\sin90^\circ=NIABτ=NIABsin90∘=NIAB
  1. Separate torque from net force. A uniform field can give a loop torque while the net magnetic force on the closed loop is zero.

Result: It is maximum.

Worked application 5: Parallel current directions

Two long parallel wires carry conventional currents in the same direction.

The wire field and magnetic force explain the interaction between parallel currents in the same direction.

  1. Find the field from one wire.
B=μ0I/(2πd)B=\mu_0 I/(2\pi d)B=μ0​I/(2πd)

  1. Apply the right-hand rule. At the other wire, use its current direction crossed with the local magnetic field.

  2. Find the force per length.

F/L=μ0I1I2/(2πd)F/L=\mu_0 I_1I_2/(2\pi d)F/L=μ0​I1​I2​/(2πd)
  1. Check symmetry. The forces point toward the opposite wires and have equal magnitudes per equal length.

Result: They attract each other.

Worked application 6: Radius of a proton helix

A proton of mass 1.673×10−271.673\times10^{-27}1.673×10−27 kg and charge 1.602×10−191.602\times10^{-19}1.602×10−19 C enters a uniform 0.010 T magnetic field at 1.00×1051.00\times10^{5}1.00×105 m/s. Its velocity makes 30° with the field. The calculation determines the helix radius. Use nonrelativistic motion.

  1. Resolve perpendicular speed.
v⊥=vsin⁡30∘=5.00×104 m s−1v_\perp=v\sin30^\circ=5.00\times10^4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}v⊥​=vsin30∘=5.00×104ms−1
  1. Balance perpendicular magnetic and centripetal forces.
∣q∣v⊥B=mv⊥2/r|q|v_\perp B=mv_\perp^2/r∣q∣v⊥​B=mv⊥2​/r
  1. Rearrange for the radius.
r=mv⊥/(∣q∣B)r=mv_\perp/(|q|B)r=mv⊥​/(∣q∣B)
  1. Substitute SI values.
r=(1.673×10−27)(5.00×104)(1.602×10−19)(0.010)r=\frac{(1.673\times10^{-27})(5.00\times10^4)}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(0.010)}r=(1.602×10−19)(0.010)(1.673×10−27)(5.00×104)​

  1. Check the other component. The parallel component controls travel along the helix axis, not its radius.

  2. State the result.

0.052216 m0.052216\,\mathrm m0.052216m

Result: 0.052216 m0.052216\,\mathrm m0.052216m

A=(0.10)(0.20)=0.020 m2A=(0.10)(0.20)=0.020\,\mathrm{m^2}A=(0.10)(0.20)=0.020m2

τ=NIABsin⁡θn\tau=NIAB\sin\theta_nτ=NIABsinθn​

Worked application 8: Zero field between unequal wire currents

v=3000/0.02=150000 m s−1v=3000/0.02=150000\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}v=3000/0.02=150000ms−1

Worked application 17: A velocity selector followed by a magnetic analyzer · the proton orbit radius in the analyzer

A beam of protons passes straight through crossed electric and magnetic fields. Their directions make the electric and magnetic forces oppose. The selector has E=4500 N C−1E=4500\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}E=4500NC−1 and B1=0.03 TB_1=0.03\,\mathrm TB1​=0.03T. The beam then enters a separate perpendicular uniform field B2=0.12 TB_2=0.12\,\mathrm TB2​=0.12T. Use proton mass 1.673×10−27 kg1.673\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}1.673×10−27kg and charge +1.602×10−19 C+1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C+1.602×10−19C. Ignore all other forces and relativistic effects. The calculation determines the proton orbit radius in the analyzer.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Straight selector motion requires electric and magnetic forces to cancel. The analyzer changes direction without changing speed.

  2. Balance selector force magnitudes.

qE=qvB1 ⇒ v=E/B1=150000 m s−1qE=qvB_1\ \Rightarrow\ v=E/B_1=150000\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}qE=qvB1​ ⇒ v=E/B1​=150000ms−1
  1. Balance analyzer force with centripetal acceleration.
qvB2=mv2/r ⇒ r=mv/(qB2)qvB_2=mv^2/r\ \Rightarrow\ r=mv/(qB_2)qvB2​=mv2/r ⇒ r=mv/(qB2​)
  1. Relate kinetic energy and period to the selected speed.
K=12mv2,T=2πr/v=2πm/(qB2)K=\tfrac12mv^2,\quad T=2\pi r/v=2\pi m/(qB_2)K=21​mv2,T=2πr/v=2πm/(qB2​)
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
r=(1.673×10−27)(150000)(1.602×10−19)(0.12)r=\frac{(1.673\times10^{-27})(150000)}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(0.12)}r=(1.602×10−19)(0.12)(1.673×10−27)(150000)​

  1. Check the physical result. The analyzer field is perpendicular to the velocity, so the full speed supplies circular motion.

  2. State the result.

0.013054 m0.013054\,\mathrm m0.013054m

Result: 0.013054 m0.013054\,\mathrm m0.013054m

Worked application 20: A velocity selector followed by a magnetic analyzer · model and interpretation

A beam of protons passes straight through crossed electric and magnetic fields. Their directions make the electric and magnetic forces oppose. The selector has E=4500 N C−1E=4500\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}E=4500NC−1 and B1=0.03 TB_1=0.03\,\mathrm TB1​=0.03T. The beam then enters a separate perpendicular uniform field B2=0.12 TB_2=0.12\,\mathrm TB2​=0.12T. Use proton mass 1.673×10−27 kg1.673\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}1.673×10−27kg and charge +1.602×10−19 C+1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C+1.602×10−19C. Ignore all other forces and relativistic effects.

The electric and magnetic forces cease to cancel for an off-speed proton in the selector.

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Straight selector motion requires electric and magnetic forces to cancel. The analyzer changes direction without changing speed.

  2. Balance selector force magnitudes.

qE=qvB1 ⇒ v=E/B1=150000 m s−1qE=qvB_1\ \Rightarrow\ v=E/B_1=150000\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}qE=qvB1​ ⇒ v=E/B1​=150000ms−1
  1. Balance analyzer force with centripetal acceleration.
qvB2=mv2/r ⇒ r=mv/(qB2)qvB_2=mv^2/r\ \Rightarrow\ r=mv/(qB_2)qvB2​=mv2/r ⇒ r=mv/(qB2​)
  1. Relate kinetic energy and period to the selected speed.
K=12mv2,T=2πr/v=2πm/(qB2)K=\tfrac12mv^2,\quad T=2\pi r/v=2\pi m/(qB_2)K=21​mv2,T=2πr/v=2πm/(qB2​)
  1. Apply the conclusion. Electric force is qE, while magnetic force depends on speed through qvB.

Result: Its electric and magnetic force magnitudes no longer match.

Worked application 21: A wire supported by magnetic force · the upward magnetic-force magnitude

A horizontal straight wire segment has length 0.3 m, mass 0.02 kg, and conventional current 3 A. A horizontal uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T makes 40° with the wire. The current and field directions give upward magnetic force. Only gravity and magnetic force act vertically after support is removed. Use g=9.81 m s−2g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}g=9.81ms−2. The calculation determines the upward magnetic-force magnitude.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Use the angle between current direction and magnetic field. Subtract weight when calculating the net vertical acceleration.

  2. Calculate upward magnetic force.

FB=ILBsin⁡θ=0.289254 NF_B=ILB\sin\theta=0.289254\,\mathrm NFB​=ILBsinθ=0.289254N
  1. Keep gravity in the net-force balance.
may=FB−mgma_y=F_B-mgmay​=FB​−mg
  1. State the levitation condition.
IbalLBsin⁡θ=mgI_{\rm bal}LB\sin\theta=mgIbal​LBsinθ=mg
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
FB=(3)(0.3)(0.5)sin⁡40∘F_B=(3)(0.3)(0.5)\sin40^\circFB​=(3)(0.3)(0.5)sin40∘

  1. Check the physical result. The magnetic force is below ILB because the angle is less than 90 degrees.

  2. State the result.

0.289254 N0.289254\,\mathrm N0.289254N

Result: 0.289254 N0.289254\,\mathrm N0.289254N

Worked application 25: A wire supported by magnetic force · model and interpretation

Reversing only the current direction reverses the magnetic force while the geometry and field stay fixed.

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Use the angle between current direction and magnetic field. Subtract weight when calculating the net vertical acceleration.

  2. Calculate upward magnetic force.

FB=ILBsin⁡θ=0.289254 NF_B=ILB\sin\theta=0.289254\,\mathrm NFB​=ILBsinθ=0.289254N

Worked application 31: Current-loop torque and orientation energy · the magnetic-moment magnitude

A rigid 20-turn rectangular loop measures 0.1 m by 0.2 m and carries 0.5 A. Its positive area normal makes 40° with a uniform 0.3 T field. Hold current constant. For orientation energy, define U(90∘)=0U(90^\circ)=0U(90∘)=0 and use quasistatic external work without dissipation. This extends the loop-torque relation by integrating it over angle. The calculation determines the magnetic-moment magnitude.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Use the angle to the loop normal. A fixed-current magnetic moment has magnitude NIA and torque tending to align it with the field.

  2. Find the magnetic moment.

μ=NIA=NIab=0.2 A m2\mu=NIA=NIab=0.2\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}μ=NIA=NIab=0.2Am2
  1. Use torque and derive orientation energy.
τ=μBsin⁡θ,U(θ)=∫90∘θμBsin⁡θ′ dθ′=−μBcos⁡θ\tau=\mu B\sin\theta,\quad U(\theta)=\int_{90^\circ}^{\theta}\mu B\sin\theta'\,d\theta'=-\mu B\cos\thetaτ=μBsinθ,U(θ)=∫90∘θ​μBsinθ′dθ′=−μBcosθ
  1. Use external work as the energy change.
Wext(θ→0)=U(0)−U(θ)W_{\rm ext}(\theta\to0)=U(0)-U(\theta)Wext​(θ→0)=U(0)−U(θ)
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
μ=(20)(0.5)(0.1)(0.2)\mu=(20)(0.5)(0.1)(0.2)μ=(20)(0.5)(0.1)(0.2)

  1. Check the physical result. Each identical turn contributes current times its enclosed area.

  2. State the result.

0.2 A m20.2\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}0.2Am2

Result: 0.2 A m20.2\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}0.2Am2

Worked application 41: Opposite currents and a third test wire · the signed y field at the stated external point

Two long wires parallel to z lie at x zero and x=0.2 mx=0.2\,\mathrm mx=0.2m. Their currents are +2 A+2\,\mathrm A+2A and −6 A-6\,\mathrm A−6A along z. The external-field calculation uses x=0.4 mx=0.4\,\mathrm mx=0.4m on the x axis. A very weak test wire there carries +1.5 A+1.5\,\mathrm A+1.5A over length 0.10 m; ignore its effect on the source wires. Use μ0=4π×10−7 T m A−1\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}μ0​=4π×10−7TmA−1. The calculation determines the signed y field at the stated external point.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Use right-hand-rule signs before adding the two wire fields. Straight-wire fields vary as inverse distance, not inverse-square distance.

  2. Write the signed field at the external point.

By=μ02π(I1x−I2x−d)=−5×10−6 TB_y=\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\left(\frac{I_1}{x}-\frac{I_2}{x-d}\right)=-5\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm TBy​=2πμ0​​(xI1​​−x−dI2​​)=−5×10−6T
  1. Find the separate zero-field location on the weaker-wire side.
x0=−I1dI2−I1=−0.1 mx_0=-\frac{I_1d}{I_2-I_1}=-0.1\,\mathrm mx0​=−I2​−I1​I1​d​=−0.1m
  1. Use current direction crossed with local field.
F3,x=−I3LByF_{3,x}=-I_3LB_yF3,x​=−I3​LBy​
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
By=−5×10−6 TB_y=-5\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm TBy​=−5×10−6T

  1. Check the physical result. The field is negative y at the stated point.

  2. State the result.

−5×10−6 T-5\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm T−5×10−6T

Result: −5×10−6 T-5\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm T−5×10−6T

The external-field calculation uses x=0.48 mx=0.48\,\mathrm mx=0.48m on the x axis. A very weak test wire there carries +1.5 A+1.5\,\mathrm A+1.5A over length 0.10 m; ignore its effect on the source wires. Use μ0=4π×10−7 T m A−1\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}μ0​=4π×10−7TmA−1. The calculation determines the signed y field at the stated external point.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Use right-hand-rule signs before adding the two wire fields. Straight-wire fields vary as inverse distance, not inverse-square distance.

  2. Write the signed field at the external point.

By=μ02π(I1x−I2x−d)=−6.25×10−6 TB_y=\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\left(\frac{I_1}{x}-\frac{I_2}{x-d}\right)=-6.25\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm TBy​=2πμ0​​(xI1​​−x−dI2​​)=−6.25×10−6T
  1. Find the separate zero-field location on the weaker-wire side.
x0=−I1dI2−I1=−0.12 mx_0=-\frac{I_1d}{I_2-I_1}=-0.12\,\mathrm mx0​=−I2​−I1​I1​d​=−0.12m
  1. Use current direction crossed with local field.
F3,x=−I3LByF_{3,x}=-I_3LB_yF3,x​=−I3​LBy​
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
By=−6.25×10−6 TB_y=-6.25\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm TBy​=−6.25×10−6T

  1. Check the physical result. The field is negative y at the stated point.

  2. State the result.

−6.25×10−6 T-6.25\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm T−6.25×10−6T

Result: −6.25×10−6 T-6.25\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm T−6.25×10−6T

Worked application 51: Infer velocity from a measured helix · the perpendicular speed

A proton follows a helix in a uniform magnetic field of 0.01 T. The helix radius is 0.025 m and the distance along the field per complete turn is 0.08 m. Use proton mass 1.673×10−27 kg1.673\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}1.673×10−27kg and charge +1.602×10−19 C+1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C+1.602×10−19C. Assume nonrelativistic motion and no other force. The calculation determines the perpendicular speed.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Radius determines perpendicular speed. Pitch divided by the cyclotron period determines parallel speed. Both components contribute to kinetic energy.

  2. Find the period from charge, mass, and field.

T=2πm/(qB)=6.56165×10−6 sT=2\pi m/(qB)=6.56165\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm sT=2πm/(qB)=6.56165×10−6s
  1. Recover both velocity components.
v⊥=qBr/m=23939 m s−1,v∥=p/T=12192 m s−1v_\perp=qBr/m=23939\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad v_\parallel=p/T=12192\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}v⊥​=qBr/m=23939ms−1,v∥​=p/T=12192ms−1
  1. Combine the orthogonal speeds.
v2=v⊥2+v∥2,tan⁡θ=v⊥/v∥v^2=v_\perp^2+v_\parallel^2,\quad\tan\theta=v_\perp/v_\parallelv2=v⊥2​+v∥2​,tanθ=v⊥​/v∥​
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
v⊥=qBr/m=23939 m s−1v_\perp=qBr/m=23939\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}v⊥​=qBr/m=23939ms−1

  1. Check the physical result. Only the velocity component perpendicular to the field bends into a circle.

  2. State the result.

23939 m s−123939\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}23939ms−1

Result: 23939 m s−123939\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}23939ms−1

Worked application 60: Infer velocity from a measured helix · model and interpretation

A proton follows a helix in a uniform magnetic field of 0.015 T. The helix radius is 0.035 m and the distance along the field per complete turn is 0.12 m. Use proton mass 1.673×10−27 kg1.673\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}1.673×10−27kg and charge +1.602×10−19 C+1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C+1.602×10−19C. Assume nonrelativistic motion and no other force.

Increasing only the parallel velocity increases the pitch without changing the radius for the same particle and field.

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Radius determines perpendicular speed. Pitch divided by the cyclotron period determines parallel speed. Both components contribute to kinetic energy.

  2. Find the period from charge, mass, and field.

T=2πm/(qB)=4.37444×10−6 sT=2\pi m/(qB)=4.37444\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm sT=2πm/(qB)=4.37444×10−6s
  1. Recover both velocity components.
v⊥=qBr/m=50272 m s−1,v∥=p/T=27432.1 m s−1v_\perp=qBr/m=50272\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad v_\parallel=p/T=27432.1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}v⊥​=qBr/m=50272ms−1,v∥​=p/T=27432.1ms−1
  1. Combine the orthogonal speeds.
v2=v⊥2+v∥2,tan⁡θ=v⊥/v∥v^2=v_\perp^2+v_\parallel^2,\quad\tan\theta=v_\perp/v_\parallelv2=v⊥2​+v∥2​,tanθ=v⊥​/v∥​
  1. Apply the conclusion. Pitch depends on parallel speed, while radius depends on perpendicular speed.
